note: First-draft identification notes written from standard public descriptions (FishBase, Wikipedia and regional field guides). None has been reviewed by a fish biologist yet. When a biologist signs one off, set expert_reviewed to true and add who and when in reviewed_by.

Coregonus huntsmani.summary: A slender, silvery whitefish of the salmon family, found only in Nova Scotia: a dark blue or green back, silvery sides and a white belly, with no spots, an adipose fin and a deeply forked tail.
features: Dark blue or green back, silvery sides and a silvery-white belly; no spots or markings on the upper body
Adipose fin present on wild fish (the small fleshy fin between the dorsal fin and the tail)
Upper and lower jaws about equal in length, with small but well-developed teeth
Deeply forked tail; dorsal and tail fins dusky
Larger scales than trout or salmon: about 90 to 100 along the lateral line (one guide gives more than 88)
Up to about 38 cm when sea-run; the landlocked Petite Rivière fish reach about 22 cm

similar.note: Lake Whitefish has fewer than 88 lateral-line scales, clear or lightly pigmented fins, a pale green-brown back (dark brown to black in some inland lakes), and may develop a hump behind the head. It is far more common, in large rivers and cold lakes across Canada, including Nova Scotia.
Brook Trout is green to brown with red dots in blue halos along the sides, and its scales are too small to count. Atlantic Whitefish has no spots.
Atlantic Salmon has black spots above the lateral line when in sea water and 109 to 124 lateral-line scales, against 90 to 100 on Atlantic Whitefish.

sources.label: Bluenose Coastal Action Foundation. Atlantic Whitefish: Identification & Status
Bluenose Coastal Action Foundation. What's the Difference? The Atlantic Whitefish versus Lake Whitefish (c. 2010)
COSEWIC (2022). Rapid review of classification on the Atlantic Whitefish in Canada (current range)

Gadus morhua.summary: A stocky, three-finned cod with a chin barbel and a pale, arched lateral line. Colour ranges from olive-green to reddish-brown, usually with fine spots.
features: Three dorsal fins and two anal fins, all rounded
Prominent barbel under the chin, about as long as the eye is wide or longer
Pale lateral line that arches over the pectoral fin
Upper jaw projects past the lower jaw
Tail is nearly square-edged, not deeply forked
Mottled or speckled sides; colour varies from green-brown to red

similar.note: Haddock has a dark lateral line and a dark blotch above the pectoral fin, and a smaller barbel.
Pollock has a pale straight lateral line, a lower jaw that sticks out and a forked tail.

Melanogrammus aeglefinus.summary: A cod relative with a black lateral line and a dark thumbprint-like blotch above the pectoral fin. The back is purplish-grey and the belly is silvery-white.
features: Dark (black) lateral line running straight along the side
Dark blotch on the side between the pectoral fin and the lateral line
Three dorsal fins; the first is tall and pointed
Small chin barbel and a small mouth with the upper jaw overhanging
Tail is slightly forked

similar.note: Cod has a pale arched lateral line, a larger barbel and no dark blotch.
Pollock has a pale lateral line, a lower jaw that sticks out and no blotch.

Pollachius virens.summary: A streamlined, fast-swimming cod relative with an olive-green to brown back, a silvery belly and a pale straight lateral line.
features: Lower jaw projects past the upper jaw
Chin barbel is absent or very small
Pale lateral line that is nearly straight
Three dorsal fins and two anal fins
Tail is clearly forked, more so than in cod or haddock
Body is more slender than a cod, with a noticeably small head

similar.note: Cod has a big chin barbel, an arched pale lateral line and a squarer tail.
Haddock has a dark lateral line and a dark blotch above the pectoral fin.

Clupea harengus.summary: A slender, silvery schooling fish with a blue-green back and a single dorsal fin near the middle of the body.
features: One dorsal fin, set about halfway along the back
Pelvic fins sit below the dorsal fin
No visible lateral line on the body
Belly has a weak saw-edge of scutes
Deeply forked tail
Scales are large and easily lost, leaving the flanks bare

similar.note: Alewife has a deeper body and a larger eye.
American shad is much deeper-bodied and larger, with a row of dark spots behind the gill cover.

Scomber scombrus.summary: A torpedo-shaped, fast-swimming fish with a blue-green back marked by dark wavy bars and a plain silvery belly.
features: About 20 to 30 dark, wavy bars across the upper back and sides
Silvery-white belly with no markings
Two well separated dorsal fins
A row of small finlets behind the second dorsal and the anal fin
Deeply forked tail with a slim tail base
Small scales and no obvious scale pattern

similar.note: Atlantic bonito has oblique dark stripes on the back and a larger mouth with obvious teeth.
Little tunny has blotchy, wormlike markings on the back and dark spots below the pectoral fin.

Pseudopleuronectes americanus.summary: A thick-bodied, right-eyed flatfish with a small mouth and a dark olive-brown to reddish upper side. The underside is white.
features: Both eyes on the right side of the body
Small mouth with thick lips
Rounded tail
Nearly straight lateral line
Upper side olive-brown to reddish-brown, sometimes mottled; blind side white
Thick, oval body compared with most other flounders

similar.note: Windowpane is left-eyed, very thin and almost see-through.
Witch flounder is more elongated and thinner, with a greyer body.

Tautogolabrus adspersus.summary: A small, hardy wrasse of rocky shores and kelp with thick lips and a long, single dorsal fin. Colour varies a lot, from brown to blue-black and mottled.
features: One long dorsal fin with a spiny front part and a soft rear part
Rounded tail
Thick lips and a pointed snout
Colour is variable: brown, grey, blue or reddish, often mottled
Rarely longer than about 30 cm and usually near rocks or kelp

similar.note: Tautog is deeper and heavier, with a blunt head and, often, a white chin.

Hemitripterus americanus.summary: A big-headed, spiny bottom fish with fleshy flaps around the head and a very large mouth. Colour is mottled red, brown, purple or green.
features: Large head with fleshy tabs and small flaps on the head and jaws
Very large mouth
Large fan-shaped pectoral fins
Spiny first dorsal fin, with a deep notch before the second
Rough, prickly skin
Can puff up with water when taken out

similar.note: Shorthorn sculpin has a smaller mouth, smooth skin and spines on the gill cover instead of fleshy flaps.

Myoxocephalus scorpius.summary: A broad-headed sculpin with spines on the gill cover, a wide mouth and big fan-like pectoral fins. Mottled brown or olive, often with darker bars.
features: Large, broad head with a wide mouth
Spines on the gill cover (the upper spine is short)
Two dorsal fins, the first spiny
Large rounded pectoral fins
Mottled brown, olive or reddish; males can have an orange-red belly when breeding

similar.note: Longhorn sculpin has a longer upper spine on the gill cover.
Sea raven has fleshy flaps on the head and a larger mouth.

Cyclopterus lumpus.summary: A rounded, plump fish with rows of bony knobs on thick skin and a sucker disc on the belly. Grey, blue-green or olive, and males turn orange-red when breeding.
features: Globe-shaped body with a high ridge along the back
Rows of bony tubercles along the body
Pelvic fins are joined into a round sucker disc on the belly
Thick, scaleless skin
Males become reddish or orange in the breeding season

similar.note: Atlantic snailfish is much smaller, tadpole-shaped and has smooth skin without the bony knobs.

Anarhichas lupus.summary: A long, tapering bottom fish with a blunt head and strong canine teeth. Blue-grey to brown with dark vertical bars.
features: Long, eel-like taper toward the tail
Large head and strong, protruding canine teeth
One long dorsal fin running from the head almost to the tail
No pelvic fins
Dark vertical bars or blotches on a grey-brown body

similar.note: Ocean pout is also elongate but has a softer head, fleshy lips and no large canine teeth.

Gasterosteus aculeatus.summary: A small, flattened fish with three separate spines along the back and a narrow tail base. Males turn red on the throat and belly when breeding.
features: Usually three sharp spines in front of the dorsal fin
A strong spine on each pelvic fin
Narrow tail base with a small keel on each side
Bony plates along the sides (often a full row in sea-living fish)
Breeding males have a red throat and belly and blue eyes

similar.note: Fourspine stickleback has four separate dorsal spines.
Ninespine stickleback has about nine small dorsal spines and a more slender body.

Fundulus heteroclitus.summary: A stocky, hardy killifish of salt marshes and estuaries with an upturned mouth. Males are darker with pale spots and a yellow-orange belly. Females are olive with faint bars.
features: Blunt, flattened head with an upturned mouth
One dorsal fin set well back on the body
Rounded tail
Males: dark body with small silvery-white spots and a yellowish belly
Females: plainer olive-brown with faint vertical bars

similar.note: Banded killifish is slimmer, with many thin vertical bars along the side.

Salmo salar.summary: A streamlined salmonid with an adipose fin. Sea-run fish are silver with dark spots mostly above the lateral line. Young fish in rivers (parr) have dark oval bars along the sides.
features: Adipose fin behind the dorsal fin
Black spots mostly above the lateral line, often X-shaped
Slender tail base; tail only slightly forked or nearly straight
Upper jaw ends about level with the back of the eye
Parr: oval dark bars along the side with a few red spots

similar.note: Brown trout has a square tail and red spots with pale rings, and the upper jaw extends past the eye.
Brook trout has pale wormlike marks on the back and pale-edged lower fins.

Squalus acanthias.summary: A small, slim shark with a spine in front of each of its two dorsal fins and no anal fin. Grey above with a pale belly, often with white spots when young.
features: Two dorsal fins, each with a spine at the front
No anal fin
Slender body with a pointed snout
Grey to brownish back, pale belly; white spots are common on younger fish

Morone saxatilis.summary: A large, silvery bass with seven or eight dark stripes running along the sides. It has two separate dorsal fins.
features: Seven or eight dark, unbroken stripes along the sides
Two dorsal fins that are separate, the first spiny
Forked tail
Olive, steel-blue or green back and silvery sides
Large mouth

similar.note: White perch is smaller and deeper-bodied, with faint stripes at most, and its two dorsal fins are joined at the base.

Morone americana.summary: A deep-bodied, silvery-grey to olive perch-like fish of estuaries and lakes. It looks like a small, plain striped bass.
features: Deep, flattened body with an arched back
Two dorsal fins joined at the base by a low membrane
Silvery-grey to olive sides, with no bold stripes
Forked tail

similar.note: Striped bass is slimmer with bold dark stripes, and its two dorsal fins are fully separate.
Yellow perch is yellow with dark vertical bars.

Alosa pseudoharengus.summary: A deep-bodied, silvery river herring that runs up Nova Scotia rivers to spawn in spring. Grey-green back and a single dark spot behind the gill cover.
features: Deep, flattened body with a sharp saw-edged keel of scutes along the belly
One dark spot on the shoulder, just behind the gill cover
Large eye, wider than the snout is long
One dorsal fin near the middle of the back; deeply forked tail
Grey-green back and silvery sides

similar.note: Blueback herring is almost identical outside. Its eye is smaller (no wider than the snout is long), its back is bluer, and its body lining is dark, which needs a fish in hand.
Atlantic herring is slimmer, with a weaker belly keel and no shoulder spot.
American shad grows much larger and usually has a row of several dark spots behind the gill cover.

Alosa aestivalis.summary: A river herring very like the alewife, with a blue-green back. Alewife and blueback are often counted together as river herring because they are so hard to tell apart on video.
features: Deep, flattened silvery body with a saw-edged belly keel
One dark shoulder spot behind the gill cover
Eye no wider than the snout is long, smaller than an alewife's
Dark blue-green back
Body cavity lining is dark, unlike an alewife's pale lining (only visible in hand)

similar.note: Alewife has a larger eye, a greyer back and a pale body lining.

Menidia menidia.summary: A small, slender schooling fish of beaches and estuaries. Almost see-through grey-green with a bright silver stripe along each side.
features: Bright silver band running along the middle of the side
Slender, translucent grey-green body
Two dorsal fins, the first small and spiny
Small mouth
Schools in shallow water near shore

similar.note: Rainbow smelt has a small fleshy adipose fin near the tail and a large mouth with visible teeth.
Sand lance is more eel-like, with one long dorsal fin, a jutting lower jaw and no pelvic fins.

Osmerus mordax.summary: A slender, silvery fish of coastal waters and rivers, with a large toothy mouth and a small adipose fin. Sides often shine pink, purple or blue.
features: Small, fleshy adipose fin between the dorsal fin and the tail
Large mouth reaching back to about the middle of the eye, with obvious teeth
Slender silvery body, often with pink or purple iridescence
Deeply forked tail

similar.note: Atlantic silverside has no adipose fin, a small mouth and two dorsal fins.
Capelin is similar in shape but has very small scales and, in spawning males, ridges of enlarged scales along the sides.

Ammodytes americanus.summary: A small, very slender, eel-like silvery fish that buries itself in sand and swims in dense schools.
features: Long, thin body
One long, low dorsal fin along most of the back
No pelvic fins
Pointed head with a lower jaw that juts past the upper
Forked tail

similar.note: Atlantic silverside is deeper-bodied, with two short dorsal fins and a bright silver side stripe.

Scophthalmus aquosus.summary: A very thin, round, left-eyed flatfish. So thin that light shows through it, which gives it its name.
features: Both eyes on the left side of the body
Body very thin and almost translucent
Nearly round outline
Front rays of the dorsal fin are long, free and branched
Large mouth
Upper side light brown with many small dark spots

similar.note: Winter flounder is right-eyed and thick-bodied, with a small mouth.

Myoxocephalus octodecemspinosus.summary: A sculpin with a very long spine on the upper corner of the gill cover. Mottled olive to brown with dark saddles across the back.
features: Upper spine on the gill cover is very long, several times the length of the spine below it
Broad, flattened head and tapering body
Two dorsal fins, the first spiny
Large, fan-like pectoral fins
Dark saddles or bars across the back

similar.note: Shorthorn sculpin's upper gill-cover spine is short, not much longer than the one below.
Sea raven has fleshy flaps on the head and rough, prickly skin.

Pungitius pungitius.summary: A small, slender stickleback with a row of many short spines along the back.
features: Usually about nine short, separate spines in front of the dorsal fin (from 7 to 12)
Slender body with a very thin tail base
A small spine on each pelvic fin
Breeding males turn black on the throat and belly

similar.note: Threespine stickleback usually has three dorsal spines and a deeper body.
Fourspine stickleback usually has four dorsal spines that lean alternately left and right.

Apeltes quadracus.summary: A small stickleback of eelgrass and salt marshes with a few long spines that lean alternately to each side.
features: Usually four spines in front of the dorsal fin, leaning alternately left and right
No bony plates along the sides
Body mottled olive-brown
A spine on each pelvic fin

similar.note: Threespine stickleback usually has three upright dorsal spines and bony plates along the side.
Ninespine stickleback has many more, shorter dorsal spines.

Fundulus diaphanus.summary: A slender killifish of lakes, streams and brackish water with many thin dark bars along an olive side.
features: Many thin, dark vertical bars along the side
Slender body, slimmer than a mummichog
Flattened head with a small, upturned mouth
One dorsal fin set well back; rounded tail

similar.note: Mummichog is stockier, and females are plainer with only faint bars.

Salvelinus fontinalis.summary: A colourful char of cold streams and lakes. Dark green back with pale wormlike markings and red spots ringed in blue on the sides.
features: Pale, wormlike markings on the dark back and the dorsal fin
Red spots with blue halos on the sides
Lower fins have a white front edge, then a black stripe
Tail almost square
Adipose fin present

similar.note: Brown trout has dark spots on a lighter brown body and no white-edged lower fins or wormlike markings.
Atlantic salmon has black spots mostly above the lateral line and a forked tail.

Salmo trutta.summary: An introduced trout with a golden-brown to silvery body marked with dark spots, often with some red spots ringed in pale.
features: Black spots on the back, sides and dorsal fin, many with pale rings
Usually a few red or orange spots on the sides
Tail is nearly square with few or no spots
Upper jaw extends past the back of the eye in adults
Adipose fin present, often with an orange edge

similar.note: Atlantic salmon has a slimmer tail base, a more forked tail and X-shaped black spots with few or no red.
Brook trout has pale wormlike markings on the back and white-edged lower fins.

Zoarces americanus.summary: A long, eel-like bottom fish with a large head, fleshy lips and long fins that run around the tail.
features: Long, tapering body
Large head with thick, fleshy lips
Long dorsal and anal fins joined around the tail
A short section of small spines near the rear of the dorsal fin
Mottled yellowish-brown to grey

similar.note: Atlantic wolffish has big protruding canine teeth and dark vertical bars, and its fins aren't joined around the tail.
American eel has a smaller head, a jutting lower jaw and a dorsal fin that starts far behind the head.

Pholis gunnellus.summary: A small, ribbon-like fish of rocky shores and tide pools, with a row of dark eyespots along the base of its long dorsal fin.
features: Long, very flattened, eel-like body
A row of about 9 to 13 dark spots, each edged in pale, along the base of the dorsal fin
A dark bar running down through the eye
Long, low dorsal fin along the whole back
Tiny pelvic fins

similar.note: Radiated shanny has a dark blotch on the front of the dorsal fin and dark lines radiating from the eye.
American eel has a rounder body with no spots, and its dorsal fin starts well behind the head.

Anguilla rostrata.summary: A snake-like fish of rivers, estuaries and the coast, with one long fin that runs from the middle of the back around the tail to the belly.
features: Long, round body
Dorsal fin starts well behind the pectoral fins and joins the tail and anal fin in one continuous fin
Lower jaw juts slightly past the upper
Small pectoral fins and no pelvic fins
Skin looks smooth; colour ranges from yellow-brown to dark olive or silvery

similar.note: Ocean pout has a large head with fleshy lips and fins that start just behind the head.
Rock gunnel is flattened, with a row of spots along the dorsal fin, which runs the whole length of the back.

Microgadus tomcod.summary: A small cod relative of estuaries and shallow coasts with three dorsal fins, a chin barbel and a rounded tail.
features: Three dorsal fins and two anal fins
Small chin barbel
Rounded tail
Pelvic fins with a long, thread-like ray
Mottled olive to brown

similar.note: A young Atlantic cod has a squarer tail, a pale arched lateral line and pelvic fins without the long thread.
Pollock has a forked tail and a lower jaw that sticks out.

Perca flavescens.summary: A freshwater perch with a yellow to golden body crossed by six to eight dark vertical bars.
features: Six to eight dark vertical bars on yellow to greenish sides
Two separate dorsal fins, the first spiny
Lower fins can be orange, especially in breeding males
Slightly forked tail

similar.note: White perch is silvery with no dark bars, and its dorsal fins are joined at the base.
Smallmouth bass is bronze-brown with fainter bars, and its two dorsal fins are joined.

Micropterus dolomieu.summary: An introduced bass of Nova Scotia lakes and rivers. Bronze to brown, often with faint dark vertical bars and red eyes.
features: Bronze to olive-brown body, often with faint vertical bars
Two dorsal fins joined, with a shallow notch between the spiny and soft parts
Upper jaw ends at about the middle of the eye
Red to orange eyes are common

similar.note: Yellow perch is yellow with bold bars, and its dorsal fins are fully separate.

Esox niger.summary: A long, slim pike with a duck-bill snout and a dark chain-like pattern on green-gold sides.
features: Dark, chain-like network of lines on the sides
Long, flattened duck-bill snout with many teeth
Dorsal and anal fins set far back near the tail
A dark vertical bar below the eye

Catostomus commersonii.summary: A round-bodied bottom feeder of lakes and rivers with a downturned, sucker-like mouth with thick fleshy lips.
features: Mouth underneath the snout, with thick, fleshy, papillose lips
Long, round body; olive-brown back and pale belly
One dorsal fin near the middle of the back
Small scales, crowded toward the head

similar.note: Creek chub has a mouth at the front of the head and a dark spot at the front of the dorsal fin.

Liparis atlanticus.summary: A small, tadpole-shaped fish with soft, loose, smooth skin and a sucker disc on the belly.
features: Tadpole-shaped body, widest at the head
Soft, smooth, scaleless skin that looks jelly-like
Round sucker disc on the belly
Long dorsal and anal fins reaching back toward the tail

similar.note: Lumpfish is rounder and much larger, with rows of bony knobs on its skin.

Merluccius bilinearis.summary: A slender, silvery hake of the shelf with a big head, a large mouth full of sharp teeth and a jutting lower jaw. It has no chin barbel, which sets it apart from the white and red hakes.
features: No barbel on the chin
Two dorsal fins, both soft-rayed; the long second dorsal is notched about two-thirds of the way back, with the rear part higher
Pelvic fins are ordinary small fins on the chest, not long feelers
Large, flat-topped head (about a quarter of the length) with big eyes; lower jaw projects beyond the upper
Dark grey to brownish above and bright silvery on the sides and belly; the shine fades soon after death
Usually about 37 cm, up to about 76 cm

similar.note: White Hake has a small chin barbel and pelvic fins drawn out into two long feeler-like rays.
Red Hake also has a chin barbel and feeler-like pelvic fins, and is reddish or olive brown rather than silvery.

sources.label: Bigelow and Schroeder (1953). Fishes of the Gulf of Maine: Silver hake

Urophycis tenuis.summary: A large, soft-bodied hake of muddy bottoms, related to cod, with a small chin barbel, long feeler-like pelvic fins and a long trailing ray on the first dorsal fin. Mature fish move inshore in summer.
features: Small barbel on the chin
Pelvic fins reduced to two long feeler-like rays, usually stopping short of the vent
Two dorsal fins: a short triangular first dorsal with one ray drawn out into a filament, and a long low second dorsal
Small scales: about 140 rows along the lateral line, the most reliable way to tell it from Red Hake
Upper jaw reaches back to the rear edge of the eye
Muddy or purplish brown above, sometimes bronzed on the sides; belly dirty white to yellowish; a dusky blotch on the gill cover
Commonly about 70 cm, up to about 1.3 m

similar.note: Red Hake has larger scales (about 100 to 110 rows), an upper jaw reaching only the rear of the pupil, a longer dorsal filament and pelvic rays that usually pass the vent. It is reddish rather than purplish.
Silver Hake has no chin barbel, ordinary pelvic fins and a bright silvery body.

sources.label: Bigelow and Schroeder (1953). Fishes of the Gulf of Maine: White hake

Urophycis chuss.summary: A smaller, reddish-brown hake with a chin barbel, feeler-like pelvic fins and a very long filament on the first dorsal fin. Juveniles live in shallow water, often sheltering in sea scallops; adults move deeper.
features: Small barbel on the chin and pelvic fins drawn out into long feelers, usually reaching past the vent
Filament on the first dorsal fin very long, three to five times the height of the rest of the fin when undamaged
Larger scales than White Hake: about 100 to 110 rows along the lateral line
Upper jaw reaches back only to the rear edge of the pupil
Reddish, muddy or olive brown above, sometimes mottled; pale belly; dusky blotch on the gill cover; pelvic fins pale
Up to about 66 cm; most are much smaller

similar.note: White Hake has smaller scales (about 140 rows), an upper jaw reaching the rear edge of the eye and a shorter dorsal filament, and grows much larger.
Silver Hake has no chin barbel and ordinary pelvic fins.

sources.label: Bigelow and Schroeder (1953). Fishes of the Gulf of Maine: Squirrel (red) hake

Hippoglossoides platessoides.summary: A right-eyed flatfish of cold, soft bottoms with a large mouth, a rounded tail and an almost straight lateral line. The eyed side is rough to the touch.
features: Eyes on the right side; large mouth gaping back to below the middle of the eye
Tail rounded or bluntly pointed, never concave
Lateral line almost straight, with only a slight rise over the pectoral fin
Scales on the eyed side have toothed edges, so the fish feels rough
Reddish to greyish brown above, white below; the tips of the long dorsal and anal fin rays are white; small fish often have a few dark spots along each edge
Usually 30 to 60 cm, up to about 80 cm

similar.note: Witch Flounder has a very small mouth, a small head, large mucous pits on the blind side of the head and a dusky pectoral fin on the eyed side.
Winter Flounder has a small mouth and a smooth-feeling body.

sources.label: Bigelow and Schroeder (1953). Fishes of the Gulf of Maine: American dab (American plaice)

Glyptocephalus cynoglossus.summary: A slim, oval, right-eyed flatfish of deep muddy bottoms, with a very small head and mouth and conspicuous mucous pits on the underside of the head. Also sold as grey sole.
features: Eyes on the right side; small head (about a fifth of the length) and very small mouth
Body elliptical and thin, two and a half to three times as long as deep
Large, obvious mucous pits on the blind (white) side of the head
Pectoral fin on the eyed side dusky to blackish
Very long dorsal and anal fins (about 100 or more dorsal rays); lateral line straight
Brownish or russet grey above, plain or with faint darker bars; usually 30 to 50 cm, up to about 60 cm

similar.note: American Plaice has a large mouth reaching below the middle of the eye and a rough-scaled eyed side.
Winter Flounder is also small-mouthed but deeper-bodied, with fewer fin rays and no large pits on the head.

sources.label: Bigelow and Schroeder (1953). Fishes of the Gulf of Maine: Witch flounder

Myoxocephalus aenaeus.summary: The grubby, or little sculpin: a small, stout sculpin of shallow coastal water, estuaries and eelgrass, with short head spines. It rarely grows past 15 cm.
features: Small: few over 15 cm, up to about 18 cm
Short, simple head spines; no long cheek (preopercular) spine, the upper one no more than twice the length of the lower
No slit or pore behind the last gill arch
Stouter than other sculpins; smooth skin; the two dorsal fins touch
Grey to greenish or brown, with darker saddles or bars; a pale band along the lower tail stalk is a useful but not always present field mark
Common in eelgrass beds and estuaries

similar.note: Shorthorn Sculpin grows much larger and usually has a pore behind the last gill arch. Young shorthorns look very like grubbies, so a small sculpin may need close examination.
Longhorn Sculpin has a very long upper cheek spine.

sources.label: Bigelow and Schroeder (1953). Fishes of the Gulf of Maine: Grubby

Syngnathus fuscus.summary: A very thin, stick-like relative of the seahorse, armoured in bony rings, with a tube-shaped snout. It lives in eelgrass and seaweed in bays, harbours and salt marshes; the male carries the eggs in a pouch under the tail.
features: Extremely slender body encased in bony rings (about 18 to 20 before the vent and 36 to 42 after)
Long tube-like snout with a tiny toothless mouth at the tip
No pelvic fins; small rounded tail fin; one dorsal fin over a few rings near the middle
Males have a brood pouch of two flaps along the underside behind the vent
Olive, brown or greenish, mottled and barred with darker; colour changes with surroundings
Usually 10 to 20 cm, up to about 30 cm

sources.label: Bigelow and Schroeder (1953). Fishes of the Gulf of Maine: Common (northern) pipefish

Gasterosteus wheatlandi.summary: A small coastal stickleback of marine and brackish water near shore, often around floating vegetation. It is easily confused with the threespine stickleback, which it lives alongside.
features: Very few bony plates along the side (about 5 or 6), against a full row in most Threespine Sticklebacks
No keel on the tail stalk
Deeper body than the Threespine Stickleback
A strong cusp above and below at the base of each pelvic spine
Green above with fine black speckling; sides golden with dark blotches; pelvic fins red in life
Typically about 3.5 cm, up to about 7.6 cm

similar.note: Threespine Stickleback usually has a long row of side plates (about 28 to 33) and a keel on the tail stalk. The two are often confused, so count the plates on fish in hand.

sources.label: Bigelow and Schroeder (1953). Fishes of the Gulf of Maine: Two-spined (blackspotted) stickleback

Leucoraja erinaceus.summary: A small skate of sandy and gravelly bottoms from the shoreline to about 90 m, with a blunt snout and small dark spots. Its egg cases ('mermaid's purses') wash up on beaches.
features: Small: usually 40 to 50 cm, up to about 54 cm
Rounded disc with a blunt snout
Adults have no thorns along the middle of the back (young do), but strong spines on the head, shoulders and sides of the tail
Fewer tooth rows than Winter Skate: about 38 to 66
Grey to brown above, often with many small round dark spots and paler disc edges; white or grey below
No eyespots on the disc

similar.note: Winter Skate usually has one to four eyespots (dark centre, pale ring) near the rear of each wing and 72 or more tooth rows, and grows far larger. A young Winter Skate without eyespots can only be told apart by counting teeth.

sources.label: Bigelow and Schroeder (1953). Fishes of the Gulf of Maine: Little skate

Leucoraja ocellata.summary: A large skate of sandy and gravelly bottoms, often in shallow water in the north of its range, usually marked with one or more eyespots near the rear of each wing.
features: Usually one to four eyespots on each side of the disc, each with a dark brown centre and a pale edge
Light brown above with many small dark spots; a pale or translucent patch on each side of the snout; white below, often with pale brown blotches
Many tooth rows: about 72 to 110
Rough back with spines on the head, around the eyes, on the shoulders and along the sides of the tail; adults usually lack a row of thorns down the middle
Large: matures at about 75 cm and reaches about 1.1 to 1.5 m

similar.note: Little Skate stays under about 54 cm, has no eyespots and has fewer tooth rows (about 38 to 66).

sources.label: Bigelow and Schroeder (1953). Fishes of the Gulf of Maine: Big (winter) skate
